regulatory_notes.when: The caller labelled the pack commercial_non_consumer.
regulatory_notes.text: Section 2(1) limits this Part to non-consumer insurance contracts. Section 3(3)(b) is about a presentation that is reasonably clear and accessible to a prudent insurer. Sections 9, 10, and 11 are about warranties and other terms. Sections 16 and 17 are about contracting out and the transparency requirements, including section 17(3), that a disadvantageous term must be clear and unambiguous as to its effect. A textual difference is not a finding that a term is disadvantageous, that section 17 was met, or that one wording is more favourable.

regulatory_notes.when: The caller did not label the pack commercial_non_consumer.
regulatory_notes.text: Section 2(1) limits Part 2 to non-consumer insurance contracts. This starter does not apply Part 2, or sections 9 to 11 and 16 to 17, as if the contract had been decided to be non-consumer, unless the caller used the commercial_non_consumer label. The label is not that decision.

regulatory_notes.when: The caller labelled the pack retail.
regulatory_notes.text: Section 61(1) applies Part 2 to a contract between a trader and a consumer. This starter does not decide that the wording is that contract. Section 62(4) is the unfairness test. Section 64(3) and section 68(1) are the transparency provisions that were read. Section 69(1) would prefer the meaning most favourable to the consumer where a term could have different meanings. This starter does not choose a meaning, does not assess fairness, and does not set favourable_to.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 2
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 2(1): this Part applies to non-consumer insurance contracts only. Section 2(2) applies the Part to variations of those contracts. This starter does not decide that a contract is non-consumer.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 3
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 3(1) is the duty of fair presentation before the contract is entered into. Section 3(3)(b) requires disclosure in a manner which would be reasonably clear and accessible to a prudent insurer. Section 3(4) is the disclosure, including section 3(4)(b), the notice that a prudent insurer needs to make further enquiries. This comparison does not decide that a presentation was fair and it does not make those enquiries.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 9
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 9 applies to representations by the insured in connection with a proposed non-consumer insurance contract or variation. Such a representation is not capable of being converted into a warranty by any provision of the contract, including by declaring the representation to form the basis of the contract. This starter records whether those words appear in a cited span. It does not decide that a clause is of no effect.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 10
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 10(1) abolishes the rule that breach of a warranty discharges the insurer's liability. Section 10(2) suspends liability for loss after a breach and before remedy, subject to subsection (3). This starter does not decide that a warranty was breached or that liability is suspended.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 11
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 11 applies to a term, other than a term defining the risk as a whole, if compliance would tend to reduce the risk of loss of a particular kind, at a particular location, or at a particular time. The insurer may not rely on non-compliance for the actual loss if the insured shows the non-compliance could not have increased the risk of that loss. This starter does not apply section 11 to a cited clause.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 16
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 16(1): a term that would put the insured in a worse position as respects representations to which section 9 applies is of no effect to that extent. Section 16(2): a term that would put the insured in a worse position as respects the other matters in Parts 2, 3, or 4 is of no effect unless section 17 has been satisfied. This starter does not decide that a term puts the insured in a worse position.

sources.title: Insurance Act 2015, section 17
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 17(1) defines the disadvantageous term by reference to section 16(2), and the page shows an amendment pointing at section 16A(4). Section 16A was not opened. Section 17(2): the insurer must take sufficient steps to draw the disadvantageous term to the insured's attention before the contract is entered into or the variation agreed. Section 17(3): the term must be clear and unambiguous as to its effect. Section 17(4) takes account of the characteristics of insured persons of the kind in question and the circumstances of the transaction. This comparison does not decide that a term is disadvantageous or that subsection (2) or (3) was met.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 61
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 61(1): this Part applies to a contract between a trader and a consumer. Section 61(2) excludes a contract of employment or apprenticeship. The page did not state an insurance-specific exclusion. This starter does not decide that a wording is a consumer contract.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 62
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 62(1): an unfair term of a consumer contract is not binding on the consumer. Section 62(4): a term is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations under the contract to the detriment of the consumer. This starter does not assess fairness.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 64
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 64(1) and (2): a term may not be assessed for fairness under section 62 to the extent that it specifies the main subject matter, or the assessment is of the appropriateness of the price, only if the term is transparent and prominent. Section 64(3): a term is transparent for the purposes of this Part if it is expressed in plain and intelligible language and, if written, is legible. This starter does not decide that a term is transparent or prominent. Schedule 2 was not opened.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 68
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 68(1): a trader must ensure that a written term of a consumer contract, or a consumer notice in writing, is transparent. Section 68(2) defines transparent for a consumer notice: plain and intelligible language, and legible. The definition of a transparent term is in section 64(3), which was also opened. This starter does not decide that section 68 was met.

sources.title: Consumer Rights Act 2015, section 69
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Section 69(1): if a term in a consumer contract, or a consumer notice, could have different meanings, the meaning that is most favourable to the consumer is to prevail. This starter does not choose a meaning and does not apply section 69. favourable_to stays null.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 5
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Article 5(1) lists the principles, including data minimisation at (c) and accuracy at (d). Article 5(1)(e) refers to Article 84B. Article 5(3) was inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. This starter copies cited lines and does not fill a gap by inference. It does not choose an Article 6 basis and it does not rectify.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 22
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. The article heading remains and the body is shown as omitted. Chapter 3 Section 4A was substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80(1), in force for this purpose from 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82). The section 80 page itself was not opened. This starter does not quote a pre-substitution Article 22 as current law.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 22A
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Article 22A(1)(a): a decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision. Article 22A(1)(b): a significant decision produces a legal effect or a similarly significant effect. Article 22A(2) says that, when considering meaningful human involvement, a person must consider the extent to which the decision is reached by means of profiling. This starter does not take a coverage decision and does not certify meaningful human involvement.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 22B
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Paragraph 1 was read: a significant decision based entirely or partly on processing described in Article 9(1) may not be taken based solely on automated processing unless one of the conditions is met. Paragraphs 3 and 4 were read. Paragraph 2 was not in the text returned on that open, so it is not quoted. This starter does not take the decision.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Article 22C(1) requires safeguards where a significant decision is based entirely or partly on personal data and based solely on automated processing. Article 22C(2) includes information, representations, human intervention, and a right to contest. This starter does not provide those safeguards and does not take the decision.

sources.title: UK GDPR, Article 22D
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. Article 22D(1) allows regulations to say when there is, or is not, meaningful human involvement for Article 22A(1)(a). Article 22D(3) allows regulations about the Article 22C safeguards. No such regulations were opened. This starter does not treat its own refusal to decide as the certification those regulations might describe.

sources.title: FCA Handbook, PRIN 2A.5
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. The page is titled consumer understanding and says it was last updated on 26 June 2026. It says a firm must support retail customer understanding so that communications meet information needs, are likely to be understood, and equip retail customers to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions, and must communicate in a way which is clear, fair and not misleading. Later text on the same page refers to that duty as PRIN 2A.5.3R(1). The page also names PRIN 2A.5.10R and PRIN 2A.5.15R. This starter does not decide that a firm met the outcome. PRIN 2A.2.5R and PRIN 2A.10 were named and were not opened.

sources.title: Harnesses in Copilot Studio
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. The GitHub Copilot harness is a Microsoft Copilot Studio authoring and orchestration framework, not the GitHub Copilot service. Customer data is not sent to or processed by the GitHub Copilot service when agents run in Copilot Studio. The page names three harnesses: GitHub Copilot, Customer Conversation, and standard. It says the GitHub Copilot harness can take a goal, break it into steps, create and edit Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF files, supports skills and memory, runs in a sandbox, and that agents and workflows on it use Copilot Credits. The billing page linked from the table was not opened. The page did not mark the harness as preview.

sources.title: Generative orchestration guidance
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. The page says the planner can invoke a topic not only by trigger phrases but also whenever its described purpose matches the user's need. It says to prefer tool names, and that names carry more weight than descriptions. It does not describe numeric routing weights. Whether the GitHub Copilot harness uses this planner was not stated on the harness overview. That link is unverified.

sources.title: Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools
sources.note: Opened 6 November 2026. The page title is Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools. It describes a cloud service with Read and Layout models for text and structure, and says v4.0 (2024-11-30) is GA. It does not name an insurance wording comparison model. The product-availability page it points to was not opened, so UK region availability is unverified. This starter does not call the service. The page uses the words Foundry Tools. It did not, in the portion read, use the current catalogue name Microsoft Foundry as the product title.

differences.from_36: Experiment 36 classifies one fact across source documents as a match, an immaterial difference, or a material discrepancy, and a reviewer resolves each material row. This experiment uses the same idea of a fixed class and a human resolution, for policy clauses. It does not import Experiment 36. A class here means the normalised text differs, or a topic is absent from one wording. It does not choose which wording is right and it does not say which is more favourable.
differences.from_37: Experiment 37 copies lines from one submission into a closed field list. A missing field is not stated. This experiment uses that citation rule across two or more wordings. It does not import Experiment 37. It does not summarise a submission and it does not price a risk.
differences.from_33: Experiment 33's resolve_span and normalise are called for each quote. A paraphrase fails. This experiment does not summarise a case bundle and does not recommend an outcome.
differences.from_12: Experiment 12 inventories the text files. No purpose is requested, so nothing is routed. A file that was not read, is outside the date window, or has a deterministic identifier finding is not quoted.
differences.from_29: Experiment 29's number and date boundary check is called. Its token-overlap verdict is not used. Support is the contiguous span. There is no threshold and no release.
